title: Exxon's Refining Profits Soared—Did Chevron Get the Same Windfall? - MarketBeat
content:
The biggest question for investors is not whether Exxon's refining business has been thriving thanks in large part to record crack spreads amid the Iran war, but how much of the earnings from these operations reached the company's bottom line, and how long that benefit is likely to last. Since competitor Chevron NYSE: CVX reported its Q3 2026 earnings results on the same day, it provides a useful point of comparison. Ultimately, Exxon's refining and marketing earnings have surpassed its upstream earnings, but the favorable mix may not continue forever. Exxon posted its largest year-to-date (YTD) refining operational performance ever, contributing to $17.5 billion in adjusted Q3 2026 earnings. Breaking down these earnings by segment shows just how dramatically refining has impacted the company's overall performance. The company's Energy Products segment includes its refining and marketing operations; this portion of Exxon's business reached $9 billion in adjusted earnings for Q3, more than double what it was last year at this time. Meanwhile, the company's upstream business, including its core exploration and production operations, came in at $7.3 billion in adjusted earnings for the quarter, down from $9.2 billion in Q2 2026. This decline was substantially wider than Exxon had indicated in its pre-earnings report. In other words, Exxon's Energy Products segment became the company's largest earnings generator for the company this quarter. While this has been a boon for the company, it leaves it exposed if fuel margins should fade. At the same time, the company still produced about 4.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day—though this is about flat on a sequential basis, it nonetheless indicates that there are not necessarily major issues with Exxon's upstream operations for investors to worry about. For this firm, production remained the largest contributor to overall earnings. Chevron's upstream operations generated about $5.7 billion in reported earnings for Q3, while its downstream operations (including refining) yielded $4.9 billion. The company also saw a heavy downward swing for its upstream earnings compared to Q2 2026, as the figure fell from $8.2 billion at that time. Notably, though, downstream earnings was essentially flat from Q2 to Q3 2026. International downstream earnings actually declined on a sequential basis, offsetting gains made in the domestic portion of Chevron's business, which processed about 1.1 million barrels per day at about 98% utilization. Russian diesel waivers and the potential for normalized Gulf shipping may help to ease the tight fuel supply in the months to come. Margins may still remain elevated, however, if geopolitical stressors continue or if refinery output from Russia remains limited. There is also strong seasonal demand to look ahead to, although a historically heavy El Niño may throw off predictions for energy usage. If margins normalize, investors will probably look more to the pace at which these firms buy shares back and how they spend their capital. Both enter the end of the year with significant capacity to generate cash. Exxon has a $20-billion 2027 buyback plan that seems to suggest management is confident the company will continue to print cash, as well as an investment program that should help to improve refinery efficiency. Chevron bought back $2.5 billion in shares last quarter, slightly lower than the previous period, but it is pushing more money toward upstream development. Investors should keep an eye on buyback plans and how they compare to distributions that are tied to temporary commodity market conditions. Additionally, diesel inventories and Russian export volumes will help to assess the impact of global conditions on both companies' margins. Alongside others in the oil and gas space, there are plenty of reasons for investors to be pleased with recent performance, although the big question is whether these companies can maintain their momentum. He highlighted ExxonMobil's 2023 Beaumont, Texas, expansion, a $2 billion project that added refining capacity equivalent to a medium-sized refinery. Woods said the investment paid for itself in roughly three years. The company is pursuing additional U.S. Gulf Coast reconfiguration projects intended to raise distillate yield by about 100,000 barrels per day. The first phase is underway at Baytown, while additional work is planned at Baton Rouge and Beaumont to increase output of diesel, lubricants and chemical feedstocks. Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Neil Hansen said diesel yield was about 3.5% higher than in 2019. He said that increase represented roughly $1.5 billion in quarterly margins this year, or $3.5 billion year to date. On a constant-margin basis, Hansen said volume and product-mix improvements combined with structural cost reductions have tripled underlying energy-products unit earnings since 2019. Woods said the company aims to provide relatively consistent shareholder distributions across commodity cycles rather than increase commitments sharply during periods of high prices and retreat during weaker markets. Hansen said ExxonMobil reduced net debt by more than $9 billion during the quarter. He said the company's financial capacity enables it to maintain capital investment and shareholder distributions through different commodity-price environments. Excluding Middle East impacts, Woods said upstream production rose year over year, supported by growth in the Permian Basin and Guyana. Production from Guyana's Stabroek Block surpassed 1 billion barrels of oil 11 years after discovery, he said. The company has three automated drilling rigs in operation and expects to expand their use to about 25% of its Permian fleet next year and about half by 2028. Woods said ExxonMobil is also pursuing technologies to improve primary and secondary recovery in the basin, with secondary-recovery opportunities expected to become more significant in the years beyond 2030. He also said ExxonMobil estimates that roughly half of Russia's refining capacity has been taken offline. He said normalization in refining markets would depend on the restoration of regional logistics, refinery repairs and potentially greater Chinese exports. title: Exxon earnings: $19B cash haul comes with a catch - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil’s (XOM) latest earnings give investors something more useful than another headline about soaring oil profits: a test of how much cash the business can generate – and how much shareholders should expect to keep receiving. The energy giant reported third-quarter net income of $15.4 billion on October 30, with adjusted earnings of $4.23 per share beating the $4.08 LSEG consensus. Refining strength helped drive the result, as disruptions to global fuel supplies boosted margins. But the investment question extends beyond this quarter’s windfall: what survives when those conditions ease? Refining reveals why Exxon is more than an oil-price bet Exxon’s Energy Products segment earned $7.17 billion, edging past the $7.09 billion generated by its upstream business. Compared with Q2, fuel-making profits increased while upstream earnings declined. That divergence illustrates the value of owning businesses across the energy supply chain. For investors, crude prices alone therefore offer an incomplete guide to Exxon’s prospects. Refiners earn money from the spread between feedstock costs and finished-fuel prices; that spread can strengthen even when oil-production earnings weaken. Integration provides another source of earnings, but unusually favorable refining conditions can also flatter consolidated profitability. Investors assessing future earnings should watch diesel margins alongside crude prices, rather than assume every business will keep contributing at today’s pace. XOM’s cash cushion is substantial – but timing helped Exxon generated $19.1 billion in free cash flow and distributed $9.4 billion through dividends and buybacks. Its reported cash generation therefore covered those payments roughly twice over, leaving considerable financial flexibility. However, working-capital movements contributed approximately $2.2 billion to operating cash flow. Excluding those movements, operating cash flow fell to $23.4 billion from $25.7 billion in the preceding quarter, even as the headline measure increased. That distinction matters because inventory, receivables and payment timing can shift cash between reporting periods without representing a lasting improvement in earning power. Shareholders still received strong cash backing for their payouts. But annualizing the headline free-cash-flow figure would risk treating a favorable quarterly movement as recurring income. The more revealing test is cash generation across several quarters, after investment needs and working-capital swings. Exxon also announced $20 billion of share repurchases for 2027, subject to reasonable market conditions. The qualification deserves attention: it preserves management’s ability to respond if the operating environment deteriorates. Buybacks can increase remaining shareholders’ ownership and support per-share earnings, but their investment value depends on the price paid and the cash available through the cycle. A large authorization alone cannot establish that shares are cheap. For prospective buyers, the strongest takeaway is Exxon’s capacity to convert favorable markets into financial flexibility. The unresolved question is how much of that capacity persists under more ordinary conditions. Friday’s results make cash coverage, refining profitability and capital allocation the measures to watch next. Those will help distinguish a stronger underlying business from a particularly lucrative quarter. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Select reference data provided by FactSet. title: Exxon CEO Says Diesel Is The ‘Key Crunch Point’ In Global Fuel Shortage – Oil Giant To Continue Investing ‘Several Billion Dollars’ In Refineries - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil (XOM) CEO Darren Woods said on Friday that global diesel supplies remain under severe pressure as geopolitical conflicts disrupt refining operations and fuel shipments, driving prices higher. In an interview with CNBC, Woods said Exxon is operating its refineries at record levels to maximize fuel production amid tight global supplies. “And frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here, because it is so critical to economic growth. Demand for diesel remains high despite capacity,” Woods said, adding that Exxon has focused heavily on maximizing refinery throughput, with refineries operating at record utilization levels and diesel yields reaching record highs. XOM shares were up 1.9% at the time of writing, hitting an all-time high. Woods pointed to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, along with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, as major disruptions to global fuel supplies. “Refining capacity is very tight today,” Woods said, adding that while crude oil supplies have somewhat recovered, refining capacity remains the biggest constraint, limiting the availability of diesel and other refined products. Woods said Exxon will continue to invest “several billion dollars” in refineries to get more diesel out into the marketplace. “Our expectation is, we’re going to increase distillate throughput by about 100,000 barrels a day, as we go forward,” Woods said. Exxon reported third-quarter (Q3) revenue of $113.16 billion, beating Wall Street estimates of $105.24 billion, according to Fiscal.ai. Adjusted earnings per share reached $4.23, exceeding expectations of $4.04. The company also declared a dividend of $1.07 per share, payable December 10. Exxon’s peer Chevron (CVX) also posted an earnings beat earlier in the day. Retail sentiment surrounding XOM on Stocktwits remained ‘bullish’ over the past 24 hours. title: ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) reports sales below analyst estimates in Q3 2026 earnings - The Globe and Mail
content: Integrated energy company ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) fell short of the market’s revenue expectations in Q3 2026, but revenue rose 29.6% year on year to $110.5 billion. Its GAAP profit of $3.72 per share was 7% below analysts’ consensus estimates. For more on ExxonMobil, read our free full research report. Cyclical industries such as energy can make mediocre companies look strong for a time, but a long-term view reveals which businesses can actually withstand and adapt to changing conditions. Over the last five years, ExxonMobil grew its revenue at a mediocre 9.8% compounded annual growth rate, falling short of the benchmark for the energy upstream and integrated energy sector. Within energy, a single time frame, even a long one, only sheds light on how well a company rode the last commodity cycle. An even longer, ten-year view helps assess whether a company compounds through cycles. ExxonMobil’s annualized revenue growth of 5.8% over the last ten years is below its five-year trend, but the results were still good. While looking at revenue is important, it can also introduce noise around commodity prices and M&A. Analyzing drivers of revenue, on the other hand, highlights what is happening inside the asset base and whether the economic footprint of a company is expanding. Over the last two years, ExxonMobil’s oil production averaged 9.9% year-on-year growth. On the other hand, its natural gas production averaged 1.1% year-on-year declines. This quarter, ExxonMobil generated a strong 29.6% year-on-year revenue growth rate, but its $110.5 billion of revenue fell short of Wall Street’s high expectations. Its oil production fell by 3% year on year. Adjusted EBITDA margin captures the operating profitability of an energy producer by removing accounting effects related to depletion and capitalized drilling costs. It reveals how much cash the asset base generates before capital structure and reinvestment requirements shape reported earnings. ExxonMobil was profitable over the last five years but held back by its large cost base. Its average EBITDA margin of 22.5% was weak for an upstream and integrated energy business. ExxonMobil’s EBITDA margin may have fluctuated slightly, but it has generally stayed the same over the last year. This raises questions about the company’s expense base because its revenue growth should have given it leverage on its fixed costs, resulting in better economies of scale and profitability. In Q3, ExxonMobil generated an EBITDA margin of 31.5%, up 11 percentage points year on year. This increase was a positive development and shows it was more efficient. Adjusted EBITDA beat Wall Street’s consensus estimates by 17.1%. ExxonMobil’s revenue and EPS both fell short of Wall Street’s consensus estimates, making this a weaker quarter with few positives. Shares edged higher 1.9% to $186.82 immediately after the report. To assess ExxonMobil as an investment right now, consider valuation and business quality as well as the latest earnings. title: XOM Q3 Earnings & Revenues Beat Estimates on Strong Refining Margins - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of $4.23 per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $3.90 per share by 8.5%. The bottom line increased from the year-ago figure of $1.88 per share. Revenues of $113.16 billion topped the consensus estimate of $103 billion by 9.9% and increased 32.7% year over year from $85.29 billion. GAAP earnings per share (EPS) rose to $3.72 from $1.76 in the year-ago quarter. The strong results were primarily driven by record refining margins, operational efficiency and optimization activities. Higher profitability was supported by strong Energy Products performance despite disruptions in Middle East production. Upstream production totaled 4,496 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day (Mboe/d). ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation Quote ExxonMobil's Energy Products segment generated adjusted earnings of $9.05 billion in the third quarter of 2026. The segment benefited from exceptionally strong refining margins as global supply disruptions constrained the availability of gasoline, diesel and other refined products. Refining capacity disruptions in Russia and the Middle East tightened product markets, supporting stronger margins. XOM's global refining network and optimization capabilities helped capture favorable market conditions. The company achieved record global diesel yields and North American diesel volumes during the first nine months of 2026. Energy Products sales totaled 5,753 thousand barrels per day (Mbd) in third-quarter. Global refinery throughput reached 3,735 Mbd, supported by strong utilization across the company's refining network. XOM's Upstream segment reported adjusted earnings of $7.31 billion in the third quarter. Higher commodity prices supported earnings, while production disruptions in the Middle East and increased depreciation associated with advantaged investments weighed on performance. The company continued benefiting from production growth in Guyana and the Permian Basin. Permian output remained above 1.8 MMboe/d, supported by technology-driven improvements in recovery and capital efficiency. Middle East disruptions constrained production availability. The company reported regional production of approximately 550 Mboe/d, while shipping restrictions delayed recognition of certain sales and revenues in the UAE. XOM Sees Support From Chemical & Specialty Products ExxonMobil's Chemical Products segment generated adjusted earnings of $725 million during the quarter. Record operational reliability and North American feedstock advantages supported profitability, although weaker chemical margins presented challenges. Chemical Products sales totaled 4,888 thousand metric tons. Strong operational execution and increased demand for high-value products in Asia Pacific supported the business despite elevated regional product availability and higher feedstock costs. Specialty Products contributed adjusted earnings of $1.28 billion, supported by favorable basestock margins. Sales volumes totaled 1,737 thousand metric tons, while the company's focus on differentiated products and structural cost reductions supported profitability. ExxonMobil's Expenses Rise Despite Efficiency Gains XOM's total costs and other deductions increased 23.6% to $91.93 billion from $74.36 billion. Crude oil and product purchases rose 37.1% to $65.72 billion, reflecting the higher cost of materials purchased during the quarter. Production and manufacturing expenses increased 11.1% to $11.22 billion from $10.09 billion. Depreciation and depletion expenses rose 5.1% to $6.80 billion, reflecting the impact of the company's expanding asset base and investments. Selling, general and administrative expenses declined 11.7% to $2.68 billion from $3.03 billion, providing some cost relief. ExxonMobil's cumulative structural cost savings have reached $16.9 billion since 2019, reflecting continued efforts to improve operational efficiency. ExxonMobil's income before taxes increased 94.3% to $21.24 billion from $10.93 billion. The improvement reflected stronger revenue generation and favorable refining conditions, which more than offset increased operating expenses. Income tax expenses rose 64.8% to $5.21 billion from $3.16 billion, reflecting higher taxable earnings. Despite the increased tax burden, net income attributable to ExxonMobil surged 104.2% to $15.41 billion from $7.55 billion in the year-ago quarter. The company's overall profitability benefited from its integrated operating model, which helped capture stronger refining margins amid global supply constraints. XOM generated $25.65 billion in operating cash flow during the third quarter, supported by strong earnings and operational performance. Free cash flow totaled $19.11 billion, reflecting cash generation after investments and other cash-flow adjustments. The company returned $9.4 billion to shareholders, including $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion in share repurchases. Cash capital expenditures totaled $7 billion, reflecting continued investments in advantaged projects and long-term production capacity. ExxonMobil expects full-year 2026 Permian production of approximately 1.8 MMboe/d. Its fifth Guyana production vessel is scheduled to begin operations late in the fourth quarter. Middle East disruptions are expected to keep approximately 350 Mboe/d offline. Higher scheduled maintenance in Product Solutions could affect performance. XOM expects full-year capital expenditures of $27-$29 billion and fourth-quarter corporate and financing expenses of $500-$700 million. The company plans $20 billion in share repurchases in 2027, subject to market conditions. ExxonMobil currently sports a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). title: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars - CNBC
content:
Chevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to full capacity to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices. Chevron shares are up nearly 2% while Exxon is more than 1% higher. Both touched all-time highs Friday. The world is facing a fuel crisis as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants attack refineries in Russia and the Middle East, reducing global capacity by millions of barrels per day. Importers have increasingly turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries for diesel supplies as a consequence. ExxonMobil’s profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, soundly beating Wall Street’s expectations. “Refining capacity is very tight today,” Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC in an interview. “Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth [with] very inelastic demand.” U.S. diesel stood at a national average of $6.32 per gallon on Friday, an increase of more than 70% compared to the same period last year, according to AAA. Prices in the U.S. hit a record high in September. Chevron’s net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, also beating the Street’s expectations of $4.89. “The system is under stress,” Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC in an interview. “We remain in an environment that is fairly fragile.” Here’s what Chevron and Exxon earned, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: High profits from the largest oil companies at a time of war is politically controversial. President Donald Trump said in August that Chevron and Exxon “were making too much money based on a shortage.” The supply disruption began in March after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. Profits from Chevron’s refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period. Chevron’s U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, Wirth said. Exxon’s refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business’ earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025. Exxon’s Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% capacity utilization. Those refineries produced “record volumes of diesel” in the quarter, Woods said. Chevron’s oil and gas production actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year. Exxon has produced about 4.5 million bpd this year, a more than 2% decline from nearly 4.7 million during the first nine months of 2025. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you.                         Patricia Miller ExxonMobil Q3 earnings beat estimates as refining profit more than doubled, offsetting lower upstream results. It also set $20 billion of 2027 share buybacks. ExxonMobil's third-quarter beat rested mainly on refining, where war-related fuel shortages lifted margins and more than doubled Energy Products earnings, offsetting weaker oil and gas production profit as prices fell. The company kept 2027 buybacks at $20 billion and extended its dividend streak, while citing geopolitical, market and regulatory conditions as risks to its plans. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation (NYSE: XOM) reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $4.23 per share on Friday, ahead of the $4.08 analysts had expected, according to LSEG data, as refining profit more than doubled from the second quarter and offset weaker results from oil and gas production. Adjusted earnings rose to $17.5 billion from $14.7 billion in the second quarter, above the $16.6 billion analysts had forecast. Net income under U.S. GAAP was $15.4 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $14.5 billion, or $3.48 per share, three months earlier. The results come as fighting in the Middle East, including the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have knocked out fuel-making capacity and caused global diesel shortages. Higher fuel prices have lifted profits across Western oil majors, and Shell and TotalEnergies also reported higher-than-expected earnings on Thursday. "Advantaged investments, technology, and $16.9 billion in structural cost savings since 2019 are expanding our earnings power. These are lasting improvements, not simply the result of favorable prices and margins," Darren Woods, ExxonMobil chairman and chief executive officer, said in the earnings release. Adjusted earnings from Energy Products, the segment that includes refining, rose to $9.1 billion from $4.1 billion in the second quarter. The company attributed the gain to higher margins and strong operations, including 100% crude unit utilization at its U.S. Gulf Coast refineries, meaning they processed crude at full capacity. ExxonMobil said Gulf Coast diesel output was the second-highest on record. It also reported record year-to-date refining performance, including its highest global diesel yield and highest North American diesel volumes, based on internal data available from 2014. Woods pointed to earlier spending on distillates, the fuel category that includes diesel. "On the U.S. Gulf Coast, investments such as our Beaumont refinery expansion have contributed to an increase in our distillate production by approximately 40% since 2019," he said. Adjusted Upstream earnings, which come from oil and gas production, fell to $7.3 billion from $9.2 billion. The company cited lower prices and an accelerated Guyana entitlement impact, which affects the share of output it receives under its contract there. Production was roughly flat at about 4.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. ExxonMobil has a higher share of production in the Middle East than its rivals. Its year-to-date results include $921 million of Middle East impacts, which the company excluded from adjusted earnings. During the quarter, the company took over as operator of the Papua LNG project in Papua New Guinea and reached agreements to increase its working interests to 34% in Papua LNG and 50% in Rovuma LNG in Mozambique, where it was already the operator. Last month it signed an agreement to explore for and produce shale in Azerbaijan, and it has held talks about a possible return to Venezuela. Chemical Products adjusted earnings fell to $725 million from $1.2 billion as margins declined. Specialty Products rose to $1.3 billion from $969 million on higher basestock margins, the base oils used to make lubricants. The gap between reported and adjusted earnings mainly reflects $2.5 billion of negative timing effects, which the company said relate largely to derivatives valued at period-end prices before the linked physical shipments are booked. ExxonMobil announced $20 billion of share repurchases for 2027, the same amount as in 2026, which it said assumes reasonable market conditions. It declared a fourth-quarter dividend of $1.07 per share, payable Dec. 10 to shareholders of record on Nov. 16, and said annual dividends have risen for 44 consecutive years. Net debt stood at $22.1 billion at Sept. 30, after a reduction of nearly $11 billion this year. The company also started up carbon capture and storage, which traps carbon dioxide and stores it underground, for steelmaker Nucor, and received approval for its Rose carbon storage project. Woods said markets will change but that the company is positioned to keep supplying energy and products while growing long-term value. Exxon Mobil Corp (NYSE:XOM, XETRA:XONA) reported third-quarter earnings of $15.4 billion, up from $14.5 billion in the previous quarter, as stronger refining margins and operational performance helped offset weaker upstream results. The US oil major reported GAAP earnings of $3.72 per share, while adjusted earnings reached $17.5 billion, or $4.23 per share, beating the LSEG consensus estimate of $4.08, compared with adjusted EPS of $3.52 in the second quarter. Cash flow from operating activities totalled $25.7 billion, while free cash flow reached $19.1 billion, up from $17.2 billion in the previous quarter. Energy Products was the strongest contributor to the sequential improvement, with earnings rising to $7.2 billion from $5.5 billion as higher margins and stronger operational performance supported results. Chief executive Darren Woods said sustained investment, operational improvements and structural cost savings had strengthened the company's earnings capacity, while helping it increase production and meet global energy demand.
